newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: AIB says Dauphin a "low risk" acquisition.
newsitem.headline: AIB says Dauphin a "low risk" acquisition.

text.p: Allied Irish Banks Plc said on Tuesday its $1.36 billion purchase of U.S. bank Dauphin Deposit Corp was a "low risk acquisition" that fit neatly into its U.S. expansion strategy.

"Our strategy is to encompass the Baltimore metropolitan area, Washington DC and the surrounding suburbs, South central Pennsylvania and Virgina. This acquisition fits very snugly into this strategy," AIB chief executive Tom Mulcahy told a news conference.
"It's a terrific deal from our perspective. It's a quality institution which ties in terrifically well with FMB and will result in FMB becoming the 45th largest bank in the whole of the U.S."

Earlier, AIB announced its U.S. unit, First Maryland Bancorp (FMB), would acquire Dauphin for $1.36 billion, a price-to-earnings multiple of 19.1 times 1996 earnings, or 2.36 times the book value of Dauphin at December 31, 1996.
Shareholders may elect to exchange each share they hold for $43 in cash, or an equivalent value of AIB's American Depositary Receipts, each of which represent six ordinary shares of AIB.

In order to preserve the tax-free nature of the transaction, a minimum 51 percent of the aggregate consideration must be in ADRS and AIB finance director Kevin Kelly told reporters a 70/30 percent mix would be desirable for the bank.
AIB, which expects to close the acquisition during the third quarter of 1997, will fund it from existing resources.

In conjunction with the acquisition, the Irish bank will seek approval from its shareholders to purchase up to 50 million of its ordinary shares in the open market to reduce its surplus capital to normal after the transaction.

Dauphin, which is the fourth largest commercial bank in Pennsylvania, has total assets of $6.0 billion and shareholders' equity of $570 million. It provides a full line of retail, commercial, trust and other financial services in south central Pennsylvania where it operates 98 branches.
It reported an eight percent increase in net income to $71 million in 1996.
AIB expected to achieve cost savings of up to $48 million per annum within two years of completion as a result of a 28 percent reduction in costs.

Cost reductions would come mainly from duplicative corporate overheads and administrative functions. AIB said it would take a restructuring charge of $60 million in 1997 to recognise the conversion and severance costs involved in this.
As a result of this, the acquisition should be earnings neutral for AIB in 1997, moderately accretive in 1998 and significantly accretive in 1999 and beyond, the bank said.

AIB said it planned to keep Dauphin's name for at least 18 months as part of its focus on customer service and retention, but declined to comment on how many jobs would go at the bank where 2,700 people are currently employed.
